title: A Bacterium That Can Grow by Using Arsenic Instead of Phosphorus
central_claims: GFAJ-1 substitutes arsenic for phosphorus for growth and incorporates arsenate in macromolecules including nucleic acids.

source_manifest.title: A Bacterium That Can Grow by Using Arsenic Instead of Phosphorus
source_manifest.finding: Original author text; central claims recorded before outcome grading.

source_manifest.title: GFAJ-1 is an arsenate-resistant, phosphate-dependent organism
source_manifest.finding: Ultrapure-media and mass-spectrometric tests find phosphate dependence and no arsenic substitution in nucleic acids; complete primary abstract read.

source_manifest.title: Absence of Detectable Arsenate in DNA from Arsenate-Grown GFAJ-1 Cells
source_manifest.finding: Purified DNA lacks detectable covalently incorporated arsenate; growth requires phosphate. Authors supplied the isolate; medium required glutamate supplementation.

source_manifest.title: Original record with formal retraction linkage
source_manifest.finding: Publisher-linked bibliographic record documents Thorp’s July 24 2025 retraction, DOI10.1126/science.adu5488.

source_manifest.title: Response to Comments on A Bacterium That Can Grow Using Arsenic Instead of Phosphorus
source_manifest.finding: Authors defend combined evidence and reject critiques as invalidating the interpretation; repository abstract read.

source_manifest.title: Growth of a Bacterium That Apparently Uses Arsenic Instead of Phosphorus Is a Consequence of Massive Ribosome Breakdown
source_manifest.finding: Independent E. coli experiments reproduce slow arsenate-associated growth through ribosome breakdown providing phosphate, an alternative to elemental substitution.

Original authors defended their interpretation. The precise 2025 retraction text was inaccessible; formal status verified via publisher-linked PubMed record, with evidentiary judgment based on the 2012 experiments.
research.summary: Independent experiments found phosphate-dependent growth and no arsenate incorporation in purified DNA, contradicting the central claim; the article was retracted in 2025. Its isolate and growth observations still motivated useful mechanistic research.
